result: Prior work has established that high-level sterile protection against malaria can be achieved through immunization with attenuated sporozoites using various approaches (radiation, genetic modification, or drug coverage), providing rationale for GAP vaccine development.
evaluation: These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to prior published work (C1-C2, C14-C16) demonstrating proof-of-concept in both rodent models (C11-C13) and humans. The claims appropriately cite established literature and provide context for the current work.

result: GAPs offer manufacturing advantages over radiation-attenuated vaccines but have faced safety challenges due to breakthrough infections in preclinical and clinical studies, particularly with the Pf∆p52∆p36 GAP, necessitating identification of additional target genes for complete attenuation.
evaluation: The claims are supported by citations to prior work (C20-C25) and the authors' own confirmatory experiments with Pf∆p52∆p36 (C24). The logical arguments about manufacturing advantages (C17-C19) are reasonable inferences from the properties of genetic modification. The conclusion that additional genes are needed (C26-C27) follows logically from the safety failures.

result: The single gene deletion mutant Pb∆b9 shows strong attenuation and induces protective immunity in mice, but occasionally produces breakthrough infections at high doses, particularly in the more stringent C57BL/6 mouse model.
evaluation: Claims C34-C41 are supported by experimental data in Table 1 showing dose-dependent protection in both BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice, with protection lasting up to 180 days but declining to 45% at 1 year. The characterization of B9 protein (C28-C29) and SLARP function (C30-C32) are supported by citations to prior work. The breakthrough infection issue (C41) is acknowledged and documented.

result: The single gene deletion mutant Pb∆slarp shows complete arrest in liver-stage development with no breakthrough blood-stage infections even at very high sporozoite doses (up to 500k), while maintaining normal blood stage growth and sporozoite production.
evaluation: Claims are supported by experimental data in Table 2 showing no breakthrough infections, Figure 1-supplement 1 showing arrested liver-stage development by in vivo imaging, and Supplementary file 1 showing normal blood stage and mosquito stage development. The safety profile is corroborated by citations to prior work (C42, C45).

result: The double gene deletion mutant Pb∆b9∆slarp shows complete attenuation with no breakthrough blood-stage infections in either BALB/c or C57BL/6 mice even after injection of very high numbers of sporozoites (150-200K), and arrests early in liver-stage development in cultured hepatocytes.
evaluation: Claims are strongly supported by experimental data in Table 2 showing 0 breakthrough infections across all tested conditions (C47, C85, C117), and Figure 1C showing arrested development in Huh7 hepatocytes (C46). This represents a clear improvement over the single Pb∆b9 mutant which showed occasional breakthrough infections.

result: Immunization with Pb∆b9∆slarp sporozoites efficiently induces sterile, long-lasting protective immunity in both BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice, with single doses as low as 1K sporozoites providing complete protection in BALB/c mice and three 10K doses providing 100% protection in C57BL/6 mice lasting at least 180 days.
evaluation: Claims are well-supported by experimental data in Table 1 showing dose-dependent protection: 100% protection with 1K-10K single doses in BALB/c (C48-C50), 100% protection with 3×10K in C57BL/6 (C51), and sustained protection at 180 days (C53). The efficacy is comparable to prior GAP and radiation-attenuated vaccines (C119). Sample sizes appear adequate (10-20 mice per group).

result: The P. falciparum orthologs of b9 and slarp show moderate sequence identity (37% and 28% respectively) and similarity (54% and 46% respectively) to their P. berghei counterparts, supporting their use as targets for human vaccine development.
evaluation: The sequence identity and similarity percentages are supported by sequence analysis data (C58-C59) and citation to prior work for b9 (C56-C57). The moderate conservation suggests functional conservation while acknowledging species differences. This provides rationale for translating the rodent findings to human parasites.

result: P. falciparum ∆slarp parasites show normal blood stage development and sporozoite production, invade human hepatocytes normally, but arrest development by day 3 post-infection with morphologically normal parasites still present at 48 hours, representing a later arrest point than Pf∆b9 parasites.
evaluation: Claims are supported by experimental data in Figure 2A showing normal gametocyte/oocyst/sporozoite production (C61), Figure 3A-B showing normal invasion at 3 and 24 hpi (C62), and Figure 3C showing >10-fold reduction at 48 hpi and complete absence by day 3 (C63-C64, C115-C116). The comparison to Pf∆b9 arrest timing (C67) is supported by citation to prior work (C65) and is a reasonable inference from the data.

result: The double gene deletion mutant Pf∆b9∆slarp was successfully generated without drug resistance markers using FRT/FLPe recombinase methodology, and shows normal asexual blood stage growth (reaching 0.5-5% parasitemia within 21 days) and wild-type-like production of gametocytes, oocysts, and sporozoites.
evaluation: The marker-free generation is supported by description of the FRT/FLPe methodology (C5, C33) and confirmed by genotyping data in Figure 2-supplement 2. Normal blood stage growth (C68-C69) and sporozoite production (C70, C89, C129-C130) are supported by experimental data in Figure 2A. This is critical for vaccine manufacturing feasibility.

result: Pf∆b9∆slarp sporozoites show normal gliding motility, hepatic cell traversal, and invasion of primary human hepatocytes, with infectivity comparable to wild-type sporozoites.
evaluation: Claims are supported by experimental data in Figure 2B showing normal gliding motility (C71), Figure 2C showing normal cell traversal (C72), and Figure 3A showing normal invasion rates (C73, C88). These functional assays demonstrate that the genetic modifications do not impair the early sporozoite functions required for hepatocyte infection.

result: Pf∆b9∆slarp parasites invade primary human hepatocytes but completely abort development, with parasites completely absent from day 2 through day 7 post-infection in two independent experiments using 40,000 sporozoites, and detailed analysis of 80 individual wells at day 4 failing to identify any developing parasites.
evaluation: Claims are strongly supported by experimental data in Figure 3C showing complete absence of parasites from day 2-7 (C74, C77, C84, C87), with invasion confirmed at earlier timepoints in Figure 3A (C6). The detailed analysis of 80 wells (C75) strengthens confidence in complete arrest. The phenotype is similar to Pf∆b9 (C124) as supported by prior work.

result: The timing of arrest for Pf∆b9∆slarp is similar to Pf∆b9, occurring early in liver-stage development.
evaluation: This claim is supported by inference from the combined day 2 and day 4 data showing complete absence of parasites (Figure 3C) and comparison to prior work on Pf∆b9 (Annoura et al., 2014). The early arrest timing is consistent with the known function of B9 in parasitophorous vacuole establishment.

result: In humanized uPA-SCID mice engrafted with human hepatocytes, Pf∆b9∆slarp sporozoites successfully infect human hepatocytes (detected by 18S DNA at 24 hours) but do not develop, showing no increase in parasite DNA at day 5 unlike wild-type parasites which show strong increases.
evaluation: While the data in Figure 3D shows the expected pattern (C78-C82), the authors acknowledge this was performed with a limited number of mice (C83). The study used only 2-3 mice per group, which is insufficient for robust statistical conclusions. The lower signal at day 1 in mutant-infected mice (C79-C80) is interpreted as reflecting early arrest, but this is speculative. Additional replicates are needed to confirm these findings.

result: Pf∆b9∆slarp completely aborted development after infection of human hepatocytes both in vitro and in vivo.
evaluation: While the in vitro data (Figure 3C) strongly supports complete arrest, the in vivo data in humanized mice (Figure 3D) is based on very limited sample sizes (2-3 mice per group). The overall conclusion of complete arrest is likely correct based on the strong in vitro data and rodent model data, but the in vivo human hepatocyte data requires additional validation with larger sample sizes.

result: Pb∆b9∆slarp represents the first completely attenuated rodent mutant with deletions of multiple genes critical for two independent biological processes: SLARP for regulation of early liver-stage gene expression and B9 for establishment of the parasitophorous vacuole.
evaluation: The claim of being the first such mutant (C90) is supported by the experimental data showing complete attenuation and the mechanistic understanding from prior work. The functions of SLARP (C91) and B9 (C92) are supported by citations to prior work (Silvie et al., 2008; Aly et al., 2011; Annoura et al., 2014). The independence of these pathways is a reasonable inference from their distinct molecular functions.

result: Complete liver-stage arrest is a critical safety requirement for GAP vaccines, but many target genes including p52, p36, and those in fatty acid synthesis show leaky phenotypes with breakthrough infections, as demonstrated by the Pf∆p52∆p36 GAP which caused a breakthrough infection in 1 of 6 human volunteers, likely due to partial functional redundancy of P52 and P36.
evaluation: The safety requirement (C93) is established knowledge. The leaky phenotypes (C94) are supported by prior work. The Pf∆p52∆p36 clinical trial failure (C96-C97, C99) is documented by citation to Spring et al., 2013. The inference of partial redundancy (C98) is reasonable given that deletion of both genes still allows some parasite development. This provides strong rationale for the multi-gene deletion approach.

result: Functional redundancy is common in Plasmodium, limiting some gene targets for GAP development: FAS II genes are essential for sporogony in P. falciparum, LSA-1 lacks rodent orthologs precluding preclinical testing, uis3/uis4 lack P. falciparum orthologs, and late-arresting GAPs may offer superior protection but carry higher breakthrough risk.
evaluation: Functional redundancy (C100) is supported by multiple citations. The FAS II essentiality for sporogony (C101-C102) is supported by citation to van Schaijk et al., 2013. The orthology issues with LSA-1 (C103) and uis3/uis4 (C104) are supported by citations and established knowledge. The trade-off between late arrest and safety (C105-C106) is supported by citations to prior work. These considerations justify the gene selection strategy.

result: Pb∆b9 elicits long-lived protective immunity but shows occasional breakthrough infections, fewer than Pb∆p52∆p36; the genes p52, p36, and b9 all belong to the 6-Cys protein family and may share similar functions in parasitophorous vacuole membrane formation, as evidenced by a triple deletion mutant being no more attenuated than the b9 single mutant, suggesting they do not drive independent pathways.
evaluation: The protection and breakthrough data for Pb∆b9 (C107-C108) are supported by prior work (Annoura et al., 2012) and Table 1 data. The 6-Cys family membership (C109) is established knowledge. The functional similarity hypothesis (C110) is speculative but reasonable. The triple mutant data (C111-C112) supporting non-independence is supported by citations to prior work. This provides rationale for combining b9 deletion with slarp deletion rather than with p52/p36.

result: The slarp mutant is the only rodent GAP with a P. falciparum ortholog that has no record of breakthrough infections in mice, with sporozoites fully capable of hepatocyte invasion and parasitophorous vacuole formation but completely aborting development soon after invasion.
evaluation: The claim of no breakthrough infections (C113) is supported by Table 2 data and review of the literature. The functional characterization (C114) is supported by the authors' data and citations to prior work (Aly et al., 2008; Silvie et al., 2008; Aly et al., 2011). This establishes slarp as an ideal second target gene to combine with b9.

result: Safety regulations require absence of heterologous DNA sequences from live vaccine strains; the FRT/FLPe recombinase methodology permits removal of drug resistance markers, leaving only two 34-nucleotide FRT sequences, and facilitates further genetic modifications.
evaluation: The regulatory requirement (C120) is supported by citations to regulatory guidance. The FRT/FLPe methodology description (C121-C122) is based on established knowledge of this recombinase system. The advantage for further modifications (C123) is supported by citation to prior work (van Schaijk et al., 2010). This addresses an important regulatory and practical consideration for vaccine development.

result: The ∆b9 attenuation phenotype induces highly effective protection but may produce breakthrough infections at low frequency; therefore, the additional deletion of slarp provides complete attenuation essential for proceeding to human trials.
evaluation: The characterization of ∆b9 protection and breakthrough risk (C126-C127) is supported by the combined rodent and P. falciparum data and prior work. The conclusion that the double deletion is necessary for clinical development (C128) is a reasonable inference from the safety data showing no breakthroughs with the double mutant (Table 2) versus occasional breakthroughs with the single b9 mutant.

result: Aseptic, purified, cryopreserved Pf∆b9∆slarp sporozoites have been produced, and preliminary data from a 6-day attenuation assay in HC-04 cells showed that none developed to mature liver-stage parasites expressing PfMSP-1, similar to irradiated PfSPZ.
evaluation: Both claims explicitly state that data are not shown (C131, C132). While the authors compare the results to prior work with irradiated sporozoites (Hoffman et al., 2010; Epstein et al., 2011), the absence of presented data makes it impossible to evaluate these claims. These are important for manufacturing and clinical development but require publication of the supporting data.
